lesson.title: Standard Form: Balancing x and y on the Same Side
lesson.summary: Standard form writes a linear equation as Ax plus By equals C, keeping both variables on one side and making intercepts especially easy to find.
lesson.body:
Standard form is another way to write the equation of a linear function, alongside slope-intercept and point-slope form. It is written as A x plus B y equals C, where A, B, and C are numbers, A and B are not both 0, and by convention A, B, and C are usually integers with A written as a positive number. Unlike slope-intercept form, standard form keeps the x-term and y-term together on the same side of the equation rather than isolating y, which is exactly why it is useful for some tasks and less convenient for others.

Any linear function can be rearranged from slope-intercept form into standard form with basic algebra. Take the line y equals 2/3 x minus 4. To clear the fraction, multiply every term on both sides by 3, the denominator: 3 times y is 3y, 3 times 2/3 x is 2x, and 3 times negative 4 is negative 12, giving 3y equals 2x minus 12. Now move the x-term to the left side by subtracting 2x from both sides: negative 2x plus 3y equals negative 12. By convention the leading coefficient should be positive, so multiply the entire equation by negative 1: 2x minus 3y equals 12. That is the standard form, with A = 2, B = negative 3, and C = 12.

Check the conversion with a specific point. In the original equation, letting x = 6 gives y equals 2/3 times 6 minus 4, which is 4 minus 4, equals 0, so (6, 0) lies on the line. Substitute that point into the standard form: 2 times 6 minus 3 times 0, which is 12 minus 0, equals 12, matching C exactly. The two equations describe the same line, just arranged differently.

Standard form shines when you need the intercepts quickly, since setting one variable to 0 isolates the other with a single step. Using 2x minus 3y equals 12, set y = 0 to find the x-intercept: 2x equals 12, so x equals 6, giving the point (6, 0), the same point checked above. Set x = 0 to find the y-intercept: negative 3y equals 12, so y equals negative 4, giving the point (0, negative 4), which matches the negative 4 constant in the original slope-intercept equation. Plotting those two intercepts and drawing a line through them graphs the equation without ever computing slope directly.

Standard form is also the natural setup for solving systems of equations by elimination, since having both variables lined up on the same side in every equation makes it easy to add or subtract equations and cancel a variable, a technique used heavily once you reach systems of equations.

Standard form can also be converted back into slope-intercept form whenever the slope itself is needed, by solving the equation for y. Starting again from 2x minus 3y equals 12, subtract 2x from both sides to get negative 3y equals negative 2x plus 12, then divide every term by negative 3: y equals (negative 2x divided by negative 3) plus (12 divided by negative 3), which simplifies to y equals 2/3 x minus 4, recovering the exact original equation and confirming the two forms genuinely describe the same linear function. Because slope is not written explicitly in standard form the way it is in slope-intercept form, it is worth remembering that the slope of A x plus B y equals C can also be found directly as negative A divided by B, which for this example gives negative 2 divided by negative 3, equal to 2/3, matching the slope found by full conversion.
